name: Croatian
family: Indo-European, Balto-Slavic, Slavic, South Slavic (western group, Serbo-Croatian)
variety: Standard Croatian (Neo-Štokavian Ijekavian norm). The codified norm has four pitch accents and post-accentual length; many educated speakers, especially in Zagreb, have stress without the tonal contrast and with reduced length contrasts.
sources: Landau, Ernestina; Lončarić, Mijo; Horga, Damir & Škarić, Ivo (1999). Croatian. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, 66-69. Cambridge University Press.
Lehiste, Ilse & Ivić, Pavle (1986). Word and Sentence Prosody in Serbocroatian. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
Inkelas, Sharon & Zec, Draga (1988). Serbo-Croatian pitch accent: the interaction of tone, stress, and intonation. Language 64, 227-248.
Smiljanić, Rajka (2004). Lexical, Pragmatic, and Positional Effects on Prosody in Two Dialects of Croatian and Serbian: An Acoustic Study. New York: Routledge.
Godjevac, Svetlana (2005). Transcribing Serbo-Croatian intonation. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology: The Phonology of Intonation and Phrasing. Oxford University Press.
Browne, Wayles (1993). Serbo-Croat. In B. Comrie & G. G. Corbett (eds.), The Slavonic Languages. London: Routledge.
Škarić, Ivo (1991). Fonetika hrvatskoga književnog jezika. In S. Babić et al., Povijesni pregled, glasovi i oblici hrvatskoga književnog jezika. Zagreb: HAZU / Globus.
Bakran, Juraj (1996). Zvučna slika hrvatskoga govora. Zagreb: Ibis grafika.
Barić, Eugenija et al. (1997). Hrvatska gramatika. Zagreb: Školska knjiga.
contrasts: four word accents in the norm: short falling (kȕća), long falling (mȃjka), short rising (vòda), long rising (rúka)
vowel length under the accent and in syllables after the accent (post-accentual length: jùnāk, genitive plural žénā)
postalveolar /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/ (č, dž) versus alveolo-palatal /t͡ɕ d͡ʑ/ (ć, đ); many Croatian speakers merge the two series
syllabic /r̩/, short or long, as a syllable nucleus that can carry the accent (krv, prst, trg, Hrvatska)
voiced versus voiceless obstruents, kept word-finally (grad [ɡraːd])
allophony: the long reflex of jat, written ije, is a diphthong or a long [jeː] in one syllable (mlijeko, lijep), not two full syllables; the short reflex je is [je]

no final devoicing; obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member, mostly shown in the spelling (vrabac, vrapca) but not always (predsjednik [pretsjednik], gradski [ɡratski]); assimilation also applies between a proclitic and its host (od kuće [ot kut͡ɕe])
/ʋ/ is a weak labiodental approximant and neither causes nor undergoes voicing assimilation
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars; /m/ is [ɱ] before /f ʋ/; /x/ is a weak velar fricative, [h]-like for many speakers
/t d/ are dental, /s z t͡s/ dental or alveolar, /r/ is an alveolar trill or tap
vowels keep their quality in unstressed syllables; short vowels are slightly more central than long ones
syllabic [l̩] and [n̩] occur in a few loanwords (bicikl, njutn)
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)V(C)(C), with syllabic r as a possible nucleus
phonotactics: falling accents occur only on the first syllable of a word, rising accents on any syllable except the last; monosyllables have only falling accents
long vowels occur in the accented syllable and after it, never before it
proclitics can take over the accent of a word with a falling accent (u grad: ȕ grād)
coda clusters are few (st, zd, št, žd and sonorant plus obstruent)

stress.type: free (lexical) pitch accent, restricted by position
stress.rule: The accented syllable is lexical; it is never the last syllable of a polysyllabic word, and falling accents are limited to the first syllable. Ordinary spelling does not mark accent or length.
stress.cues: pitch pattern over the accented and the following syllable, duration, and intensity; vowel quality does not change

rhythm.notes: Often described as syllable-timed with added phonemic length; the class label is an impression from the descriptive literature.

length.notes: Long accented vowels are about one and a half times as long as short accented ones (Lehiste & Ivić 1986); post-accentual long vowels are shorter than accented long vowels and are often shortened or lost in urban Croatian speech.

intonation.declarative: each accented word carries its lexical accent shape; successive peaks are downstepped and the phrase ends low
intonation.yes_no_question: questions with the particle li or with je li, da li end low like statements, with the verb or the focus high; questions marked by intonation alone have a low accented syllable on the focused word and a high peak on the next syllable whatever the lexical accent (Lehiste & Ivić's reverse pattern)
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: falling accents: peak at the start of the accented syllable, low afterwards; rising accents: low to rising pitch on the accented syllable with the peak on the following syllable
intonation.notes: In speech without the tonal contrast (for example Zagreb) every accented syllable has a high or rising-falling pitch.

inventory.name: short falling (kratkosilazni), marked ȁ
inventory.description: short accented vowel with the pitch peak at its beginning and a fall; the following syllable is low. Only on first syllables and monosyllables

inventory.name: long falling (dugosilazni), marked ȃ
inventory.description: long accented vowel with an early peak and a fall through the vowel; the following syllable is low. Only on first syllables and monosyllables

inventory.name: short rising (kratkouzlazni), marked à
inventory.description: short accented vowel with level or slightly rising pitch; the following syllable is as high or higher and carries the fall. Never on the last syllable

inventory.name: long rising (dugouzlazni), marked á
inventory.description: long accented vowel with pitch rising through the vowel; the following syllable starts high and then falls. Never on the last syllable

sandhi: a proclitic before a word with a falling accent can take over the accent, as falling or as rising according to the word class (u grad: ȕ grād; ne znam: nè znām)
in intonation questions the lexical accent shapes are replaced by one low-high pattern on the focused word
tone.neutral_tone: syllables before the accent are mid; syllables after a falling accent are low; the first syllable after a rising accent is high and the rest are low
tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the descriptions in Lehiste & Ivić (1986) and Inkelas & Zec (1988), not measured values. In tonal analyses a rising accent is a high tone on the syllable after the stressed one, a falling accent a high tone on the stressed (first) syllable itself.

problems: No pitch accent: the four accents are not distinguished and there are no tone phonemes. Accent marks in the text are ignored (kȕća, vòda, mâjka, grȃd read like the unmarked words), except that acute-marked vowels are read as long (rúka).
No vowel length: the rules and word list give long vowels in a handful of words only (Hrvatska), so accented and post-accentual length are missing.
Stress is always on the first syllable. That is right for falling accents but wrong for words with a rising accent on a later syllable (ljepòta, telèvīzija, interesàntan, Jugòslāvija).

Syllabic r between consonants is a plain consonant (phoneme R2) and not a syllable nucleus: krv, prst, trg, vrt, smrt come out with no stressed syllable at all, and prvi, crkva, brzo, vrlo are stressed on the last vowel.
Unstressed /a i u/ are replaced by reduced qualities (& [æ]-like, [ɪ], [ʊ]); the standard has no vowel reduction.
The long jat reflex ije is read as two syllables [i.je] (mlijeko, lijep, dijete).
The letter e is open-mid [ɛ] but close [e] after j, which has no basis in the language.
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: č and ć, dž and đ are kept apart
no final devoicing (grad, hleb keep voiced consonants)
regressive voicing assimilation, also between words (od kuće [ot], predsjednik, gradski)
lj and nj as single palatals [ʎ ɲ]; [ŋ] before velars
Cyrillic input is converted to Latin

notes: Croatian, Bosnian and Serbian share one set of rule and list files in eSpeak NG (hr_rules, sr_rules and bs_rules are identical, with conditional entries ?1 to ?4); the voices differ in phoneme table and voice settings. No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence; Bakran (1996) reports formant measurements for Croatian vowels.
